This topic is bringing out the hallucination-panic crowd.

It's perfectly safe to use LLMs to surface underlying data and knowledge without having to trust that it's giving you correct advice.

Use the LLM as search technology: string match -> semantic search -> search intelligence.

This is especially helpful when you don't know the right question to ask. Semantics only help you find text that is semantically near the input query. Semantics won't help you when what you are looking for is connected to what you have by something other than semantics, like causation, mechanism, or interpretation.

Trying to figure out why your crops aren't growing well will likely require you to read several articles across a range of sciences, probably scoped to the specific conditions you are dealing with. A semantic search is not going to surface those first.

Allowing an LLM to chain together several sources for you to read first does not require you to ask it for a conclusion.

The readme on Github does say the system produces hallucinated sources https://github.com/anonnerdfrenzy/survival-llm#how-the-model..., but really you're correct, for this kind of highly targeted use case the LLM's summary could probably be ignored entirely and the system could work extremely well even just as a search engine: index all of the content up front, chunked by paragraph and maybe enriched with a HyDE step, have the LLM facilitate running a handful of hybrid keyword/semantic searches based on the user's question and reranking the results, and show the exact pieces of text in the corpus that are most responsive to their question. No summary needed.
Not sure what the LLM is adding there then other than injecting a step into your search that could hallucinate.

Query expansion and reranking are both valuable and things that even small LLMs are pretty good at. People are broadly not great at writing search queries, so a system that takes a poorly phrased question, turns it into several different actual search queries and then merges and sorts the results by relevance can have a big impact. All the better if the AI can ask the user some clarifying questions.

The issue is the opposite of hallucinations where the LLM ignores relevant information.

Sure you can combine this with a regular search but there’s opportunity cost whenever you say LLM + something else rather than just the other thing.

Multiple times yesterday I caught Claude giving slightly incorrect information about things it had read in docs and source code. Its info was accurate enough to be plausible, but it was still wrong. And when I pointed that out, it agreed that it had overstated or made statements without verifying them.

It would be terrible to be doing an emergency medical procedure and have an AI backtrack on something it had told you to do.
I literally just said that you should let the AI surface the information for you -- not summarize or draw a conclusion for you.

There's this article on a woman dying after ChatGPT "helped" her taper off medication https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/27/well/ai-chatgpt-medicatio...

There really needs to be some kind of "double check" mechanism built into these things instead of putting 100% of that on the consumer. Humans simply don't have the mental capacity to double check the amount of data coming out of LLMs.

The "double check" mechanism for medications is: We tell people not to take medical advice from anyone who is not trained in medicine.

This is not a new problem. The internet has been full of nonsense since the 1990s (at least). Gossip and malicious rumors are as old as language.

It is not realistic to stop the generation of nonsense (of the malicious or the stupid sort). We should train people to detect and ignore nonsense when they hear it.

The difference is back then we had the adage "don't believe everything you read online" that helped adjust our priors. Today, however, these companies are specifically marketing themselves as the source of ground truth. Your boss, or your school that a generation ago banned wikipedia, is now demanding you to use these tools and make the work dependent on them.

This advice is inadequate and impractical. Most people don't have access to doctors who spend enough time on them to really get to the bottom of all issues.

In most countries, there are simply too many patients per doctor, meaning it's a conveyor belt of "good enough" 5 minute appointments.

People will turn to other modes of discussing and analyzing their problems if they go to professionals repeatedly and the problem still isn't solved. Just telling them not to do so or to ignore 100% of it isn't going to solve that.

> It is not realistic to stop the generation of nonsense (of the malicious or the stupid sort).

Seems like a big statement. Why is it not realistic? People are already doing it manually by having one LLM fact check output from another.

You can of course condense down critical information into a survival handbook, but in existential crises you don't necessarily know in advance what you'll need to know. Wikipedia (as a benchmark repository of knowledge) is ~5 million pages and would require a decent-size room to store if printed out. By contrast, a laptop + solar panel can fit in a backpack. SD cards/USB sticks with the capacity to store all of Wikipedia are a few $ each.

If things are so bad that you need to factor in the non-operability of any electronic devices, how many indestructible paper libraries are you planning to build and manage in advance, and at what budget?

I don't think Wikipedia is a good benchmark here. Try 30 random articles and see how much of that information you would want to have with you in an emergency survival scenario.

Either way the comparisons here are unfair. An LLM that runs off a backpack-sized solar panel and a laptop might be a substitute for a broad, low quality, surface-level encyclopedia but it's many orders of magnitude worse than a library of books.

I would argue that in a survival situation the accuracy of information becomes even more important. If an LLM to misidentifies a plant (or a medical condition, its treatment, etc.) it could put you in an ER, but in a survival situation that could kill you.

It's not important that it's Wikipedia specifically; I just picked that as a benchmark because it's large and comprehensive. The point is that you can't carry a library of books around easily.

You're arguing from two opposite positions. On the one hand you want information that's relevant to an emergency survival situation, presumably specific instructions on on emergency medical procedures or protection against hazards.

On the other hand you are also arguing for a physical library of books, which requires a building to house safely (and a structurally sound building, not on where the roof can fall in and the books are quickly lost to damp/fire/wildlife) and a full size cargo container if you want to move it around.

If you can maintain a physical library safely enough to hedge against the risks of it being your only library for the foreseeable future, you can probably also maintain a hospital and essential infrastructure of civilization. You're operating something equivalent to a small university campus with a high degree of physical security even if you've had to fall back on 19th century technology because power and water infrastructure have collapsed. Perhaps people are investing in that sort of thing as a hedge against a Carrington event or other abrupt technological collapse, but I'm not aware of any organized effort to build a network of knowledge-preserving monasteries at fairly significant expense for each one.

A digital encyclopaedia/library isn't ideal by any means, but it's portable and maintainable at low cost, for individuals or groups. In the space/weight that a single large book takes up, you can fit abundant storage, several e-ink readers (which will probably last very well given their low power consumption), a battery, a large solar collection sheet, and and a faraday bag to store it all in, for under $1000.

There are a fair number of people who seem to believe that LLMs contain "world knowledge" and are blissfully unaware of how inaccurate an ungrounded chatbot can be. They ask it questions, it gives them confident and plausible (sometimes even correct!) answers, and they leap to the conclusion that these are useful tools for end-of-civilization knowledge bases. I fought this battle countless times on HN and Reddit, generally unsuccessfully.

This project at least attempts to ground its answers with (presumably) human-vetted sources. That will make it much, MUCH more accurate and truthful than a bare model. But there is still a non-zero chance for it to hallucinate answers, especially when posed a question that it doesn't have any source material in its database.

As for why bother hooking up an LLM instead of a simple search engine, search engines don't synthesize data from multiple sources into a coherent answer for you, but LLMs are (mostly) great at that.

That said, while I like this pattern (LLM + knowledge base) for lots of things, this isn't necessarily something I'd trust with my own (or my family's) survival.
